feedback: If a learner thinks the marked coil travels to the far end, replay slowly and watch only the tape — the coil returns to its starting spot while the compression moves on.
Connect the diagram to the graph: the peak of the pressure graph should sit above the densest band of particles.
activities.intendedInsight: A longitudinal sound wave transfers energy along the medium while each particle oscillates in place; compressions and rarefactions correspond to high- and low-pressure regions.
learnerActions: Stretch a long slinky along a smooth floor or table with a partner.
Push and pull one end sharply to send a compression pulse travelling to the far end (a longitudinal pulse, not a side-to-side wiggle).
Mark one coil with tape and watch it carefully: note that it only jiggles back and forth about its own spot while the squashed-together region travels the whole length.
Draw a particle-line diagram beneath a pressure-vs-position graph: dense bands = compressions (particles bunched, high pressure); sparse bands = rarefactions (particles spread, low pressure).
State in your own words what moves along the slinky and what does not.
activities.title: Slinky model: energy travels, matter stays

feedback: If a learner says the bell simply stopped ringing, draw attention to the still-visibly-striking hammer — the source is unchanged; what changed is the medium.
Credit learners who note the experiment's limits (no perfect vacuum, solid-borne vibration) rather than treating the demo as proving absolute silence.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound needs a medium: as particles are removed the disturbance has less to travel through, so the sound fades even while the source still vibrates — which is why space is silent.
learnerActions: Observe a bell or buzzer with a visible striking hammer mounted inside a sealed jar connected to a vacuum pump.
Before pumping, predict what will happen to the sound and to the visible striking as air is removed, and give a reason.
Watch and listen as air is withdrawn: note that the hammer keeps visibly striking while the sound fades.
Explain the result using particles: with fewer particles there is less to carry the disturbance onward.

Discuss the honest caveat: a real pump never reaches a perfect vacuum, and vibration can travel through the mounting, so the bell is suspended on something elastic — it is the fading as pressure falls, not total silence, that carries the argument.
activities.title: Bell jar: fading to silence as air leaves

feedback: If a learner treats an echo as a separate mystery, restate it as the same sound bouncing back after a delay.
If a learner says absorbed sound 'disappears', correct to energy being transferred to the material — this is why soft furnishings cut echoes.
For the foam question, separate transmission from absorption: foam is porous and absorbs, which is different from a hard solid transmitting sound well.
activities.intendedInsight: An echo is simply reflected sound (usable for ranging), while absorption transfers sound energy into a soft material rather than reflecting or destroying it — so hard-walled rooms tend to ring with echoes and soft-furnished rooms tend to have fewer echoes.
learnerActions: Describe an echo as sound reflected off a surface and heard again after a delay.
Work out how timing a reflected pulse's return gives distance: the sound travels there and back, so distance = speed × time ÷ 2. Link this to real uses: sonar, depth-sounding, and ultrasound scans.
Compare a bare, hard-walled hall (sound rings) with a carpeted, curtained room (sound is 'dead') and explain the difference.
Explain absorption as energy transfer: soft/porous materials convert sound energy (warming slightly) rather than destroying it, which reduces echoes.
Answer: if solids carry sound well, why does studio foam reduce echoes rather than amplify them?
activities.title: Echoes and absorption: reflected sound at work

feedback: If a learner expects to hear sound in space, link back to the bell jar: no particles means nothing to carry the disturbance, even though light still reaches us.
activities.intendedInsight: Sound is a mechanical wave requiring a medium, whereas light is electromagnetic and travels through a vacuum — a clean contrast that cements why a medium is essential for sound.
learnerActions: Contrast two everyday facts: we can see the Sun across empty space but could not hear an explosion there.
State which wave needs a medium (sound, mechanical) and which does not (light, electromagnetic).
Use this contrast to justify why space is silent, connecting back to the bell-jar result.
activities.title: Sound versus light: which needs a medium?
